title: The Lawsuits That Could Change Social Media Forever w/ Ben Zipursky
summary: Benjamin Zipursky separates negligence, consumer fraud, product liability and public nuisance in social-media litigation. He favors ordinary negligence while criticizing expansive nuisance theories and emphasizing federal defenses and appeals. Eisman identifies lasting legal exposure and possible product changes. Later multistate settlements, New Mexico remedies and continuing trials support material risk, but do not establish every causal allegation. The guest misstates the California damages split; Eisman overstates the absence of related appellate precedent and assumes all cases will be appealed. The New Mexico court later rejected direct algorithm redesign while ordering other safeguards and abatement funding.
assessment: The central warning about prolonged and potentially substantial exposure has meaningful support. Legal opinions about the proper scope of nuisance are normative, not failed forecasts because a trial judge ruled differently. Preserve the distinction between alleged harm, adjudicated facts, settlement obligations and final appellate outcomes.
speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_01 is Steve Eisman; SPEAKER_00 is Fordham tort scholar Benjamin (Ben) Zipursky, established by introduction and legal answers. Short embedded interjections are attributed from dialogue.
framework_points: Classify cause of action, plaintiff and remedy before assessing exposure.
Separate third-party publication from a platform's independent design duties.
Distinguish complaints, jury findings, judgments, settlement and appeals.
Consider aggregated state exposure rather than only one verdict.
Separate a normative legal critique from a prediction of judicial outcomes.
Preserve alternative causes and uncertainty about technical implementation.
Update legislative pessimism when state activity supplies contrary evidence.
tools_and_charts: Negligence, strict product liability and consumer-protection claims
First Amendment and Supreme Court review
Corporate cash flow versus aggregate litigation exposure
transcript_cautions: Publication is June 17, but discussion says the May 4 bench trial began last week. Recording in early May is an inference, not an exact verified date.
Ziperski is normalized to Zipursky from the named Fordham scholar.
Eisman briefly says Arizona while repeatedly discussing New Mexico; the substantive case mapping uses the established New Mexico context.
The guest explicitly has not carefully read the New Mexico pleadings and gives tentative accounts of jury motives and plaintiff history.
The spoken California damages split of $4 million compensatory and $2 million punitive conflicts with the filed $3 million compensatory award.
A no-appellate-decisions statement is narrower when applied to the new verdicts than when applied to related Section 230 design issues.
The court's August algorithm-relief rejection is distinct from its other product safeguards and abatement award; Meta later reported a stay.
